subproblems.statement: Let m, q ∈ ℕ, X ∈ D_q(ℝ^m) and Z ∈ D_{q+1}(ℝ^{m+1}) with ProdChar(X, Z). Let η, η′ ∈ D^{q+1}(ℝ^{m+1}) and let N ⊆ ℝ^{m+1} be an open set with cyl(spt X) ⊆ N and η(y) = η′(y) for every y ∈ N. Then Z(η) = Z(η′). (No finiteness of M(X) is assumed.) Notation: ℝ^p := Eucl p = EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin p). For s ∈ ℝ and x ∈ ℝ^m, cons(s, x) := (EuclideanSpace.equiv (Fin (m+1)) ℝ).symm (Fin.cons s (EuclideanSpace.equiv (Fin m) ℝ x)) ∈ ℝ^{m+1}; ι(v) := cons(0, v); e₀ := EuclideanSpace.single 0 1 ∈ ℝ^{m+1}; for y ∈ ℝ^{m+1}, t(y) := EuclideanSpace.equiv (Fin (m+1)) ℝ y 0 and tl(y) := (EuclideanSpace.equiv (Fin m) ℝ).symm (Fin.tail (EuclideanSpace.equiv (Fin (m+1)) ℝ y)); cyl(A) := {y : t(y) ∈ [0,1] ∧ tl(y) ∈ A}. D_q(ℝ^p) := GeometricCurrentOn univ q, D^q(ℝ^p) := TestFormOn univ q, M = mass, spt = support, |γ| := covectorEuclideanNorm γ. For X ∈ D_q(ℝ^m) and Z ∈ D_{q+1}(ℝ^{m+1}), ProdChar(X, Z) means: for every η ∈ D^{q+1}(ℝ^{m+1}) and every φ : ℝ → D^q(ℝ^m) with φ(s)(x)(v) = η(cons(s, x))(Fin.cons e₀ (i ↦ ι(v_i))) for all s ∈ [0,1], x ∈ ℝ^m and v : Fin q → ℝ^m, one has Z(η) = ∫_0^1 X(φ(s)) ds (interval integral).

Notation: ℝ^p := Eucl p = EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin p). For s ∈ ℝ and x ∈ ℝ^m, cons(s, x) := (EuclideanSpace.equiv (Fin (m+1)) ℝ).symm (Fin.cons s (EuclideanSpace.equiv (Fin m) ℝ x)) ∈ ℝ^{m+1}; ι(v) := cons(0, v); e₀ := EuclideanSpace.single 0 1 ∈ ℝ^{m+1}; for y ∈ ℝ^{m+1}, t(y) := EuclideanSpace.equiv (Fin (m+1)) ℝ y 0 and tl(y) := (EuclideanSpace.equiv (Fin m) ℝ).symm (Fin.tail (EuclideanSpace.equiv (Fin (m+1)) ℝ y)); cyl(A) := {y : t(y) ∈ [0,1] ∧ tl(y) ∈ A}. D_q(ℝ^p) := GeometricCurrentOn univ q, D^q(ℝ^p) := TestFormOn univ q, M = mass, spt = support, |γ| := covectorEuclideanNorm γ. For X ∈ D_q(ℝ^m) and Z ∈ D_{q+1}(ℝ^{m+1}), ProdChar(X, Z) means: for every η ∈ D^{q+1}(ℝ^{m+1}) and every φ : ℝ → D^q(ℝ^m) with φ(s)(x)(v) = η(cons(s, x))(Fin.cons e₀ (i ↦ ι(v_i))) for all s ∈ [0,1], x ∈ ℝ^m and v : Fin q → ℝ^m, one has Z(η) = ∫_0^1 X(φ(s)) ds (interval integral). For s ∈ ℝ let j_s(x) := cons(s, x).

1. (Coordinate identities.) For s ∈ ℝ and x ∈ ℝ^m: t(cons(s, x)) = s and tl(cons(s, x)) = x. Indeed EuclideanSpace.equiv applied to (EuclideanSpace.equiv).symm f returns f (ContinuousLinearEquiv.apply_symm_apply); then (Fin.cons s g) 0 = s (Fin.cons_zero) and Fin.tail (Fin.cons s g) = g (Fin.tail_cons); finally (EuclideanSpace.equiv (Fin m) ℝ).symm (EuclideanSpace.equiv (Fin m) ℝ x) = x (ContinuousLinearEquiv.symm_apply_apply). Consequently, if s ∈ [0,1] and x ∈ spt X, then cons(s, x) ∈ cyl(spt X).
2. (Slice families.) Apply slice_forms (with P := m and m := q) to η and to η′. This gives φ, φ′ : ℝ → D^q(ℝ^m) with φ(s)(x)(v) = η(cons(s, x))(Fin.cons e₀ (i ↦ ι(v_i))) and φ′(s)(x)(v) = η′(cons(s, x))(Fin.cons e₀ (i ↦ ι(v_i))) for all s ∈ ℝ, x ∈ ℝ^m and v : Fin q → ℝ^m. (The joint continuity also provided by slice_forms is not needed.)
3. (Product characterization.) The identities of step 2 hold in particular for s ∈ [0,1], so ProdChar(X, Z) applied to (η, φ) and to (η′, φ′) gives Z(η) = ∫_0^1 X(φ(s)) ds and Z(η′) = ∫_0^1 X(φ′(s)) ds.
4. (The integrands agree on [0,1].) Fix s ∈ [0,1].
   (a) j_s is continuous: x ↦ Fin.cons s (EuclideanSpace.equiv (Fin m) ℝ x) is continuous (a constant first entry and a continuous linear map; Continuous.finCons), and (EuclideanSpace.equiv (Fin (m+1)) ℝ).symm is a continuous linear equivalence. Hence N_s := j_s⁻¹(N) is open.
   (b) spt X ⊆ N_s: for x ∈ spt X, cons(s, x) ∈ cyl(spt X) ⊆ N by step 1 and the hypothesis cyl(spt X) ⊆ N.
   (c) For x ∈ N_s the point y := cons(s, x) lies in N, so η(y) = η′(y). Hence for every v, φ(s)(x)(v) = η(y)(Fin.cons e₀ (i ↦ ι(v_i))) = η′(y)(Fin.cons e₀ (i ↦ ι(v_i))) = φ′(s)(x)(v), i.e. φ(s)(x) = φ′(s)(x) (extensionality of continuous alternating maps).
   (d) locality, applied with P := m, n := q, U := univ, T := X, ψ := φ(s), φ := φ′(s) and the open set N_s ⊇ spt X, gives X(φ(s)) = X(φ′(s)).
5. (Conclusion.) The functions s ↦ X(φ(s)) and s ↦ X(φ′(s)) agree on [0,1] = uIcc 0 1 (Set.uIcc_of_le), so intervalIntegral.integral_congr gives ∫_0^1 X(φ(s)) ds = ∫_0^1 X(φ′(s)) ds; no integrability is needed. By step 3, Z(η) = Z(η′). ∎

subproblems.title: Interior-product and pull-back bound |γ(w, T·, …, T·)| ≤ √(k+1)·|w|·‖T‖^k·|γ| (fact (F8))
subproblems.statement: Let m, m′, k ∈ ℕ, let γ be a (k+1)-covector on ℝ^{m′} (γ : Covector (Eucl m′) (k+1)), w ∈ ℝ^{m′}, T : ℝ^m → ℝ^{m′} a continuous linear map, a ∈ ℝ, and let β be a k-covector on ℝ^m with β(v) = a·γ(Fin.cons w (i ↦ T(v_i))) for every v : Fin k → ℝ^m. Then |β| ≤ |a|·√(k+1)·‖w‖·‖T‖^k·|γ|. Here |·| = covectorEuclideanNorm, the Euclidean norm of the coefficients α(e_{I(1)}, …, e_{I(n)}) over strictly increasing index tuples I (e = standard basis, EuclideanSpace.basisFun), ‖w‖ is the Euclidean norm and ‖T‖ the operator norm.

Source: (F8) in Part 2 of the supplied proof of dph_smooth_homotopy, with (F7) taken from the accepted sibling pullback_norm. The supplied proof bounds the contraction γ_w := γ(w, ·) by counting coefficients, which gives the constant √(m′^k)·√m′ and needs that every value γ(e_i, e_J) is ± a coefficient of γ. Here that step is replaced by Cauchy–Schwarz together with the accepted all-tuples identity tuple_sum_factorial. This avoids sorting index tuples and gives the constant √(k+1); the sibling affine_estimate only needs some constant depending on (m′, k). Siblings used: pullback_norm (iwl_sp_covectorEuclideanNorm_pullback_le) and tuple_sum_factorial (iwl_sp_pn_sum_sq_tuples_eq_factorial_mul).

Notation: for an n-covector α on ℝ^p, |α| := covectorEuclideanNorm α = √(Σ_{I : Fin n → Fin p strictly increasing} α(e∘I)²), where e_b := EuclideanSpace.basisFun (Fin p) ℝ b and e∘I := (i ↦ e_{I(i)}). Below e_b is the standard basis of ℝ^{m′}, and w_b is the b-th coordinate of w.

1. (The contraction.) Let γ_w := γ.curryLeft w (ContinuousAlternatingMap.curryLeft), a k-covector on ℝ^{m′} with γ_w(u) = γ(Matrix.vecCons w u) = γ(Fin.cons w u) for every u : Fin k → ℝ^{m′} (ContinuousAlternatingMap.curryLeft_apply_apply; Matrix.vecCons is Fin.cons). Then β = a • (γ_w.compContinuousLinearMap T), because at every v both sides equal a·γ(Fin.cons w (i ↦ T(v_i))).
2. (Homogeneity.) For every n-covector α on ℝ^p and c ∈ ℝ, |c•α| = |c|·|α|: each term of the defining sum is multiplied by c², so |c•α| = √(c²·S) = √(c²)·√S = |c|·|α| (Real.sqrt_mul with c² ≥ 0, Real.sqrt_sq_eq_abs), where S is the defining sum of α. By step 1, |β| = |a|·|γ_w.compContinuousLinearMap T|.
3. (Pull-back.) pullback_norm with P := m, Q := m′, j := k, L := T and α := γ_w gives |γ_w.compContinuousLinearMap T| ≤ ‖T‖^k·|γ_w|.
4. (Expansion in the first slot.) w = Σ_b w_b·e_b (OrthonormalBasis.sum_repr for EuclideanSpace.basisFun, whose coordinates are the w_b). Since γ.curryLeft is linear, γ_w = Σ_b w_b • γ.curryLeft(e_b), so γ_w(u) = Σ_b w_b·γ(Fin.cons e_b u) for every u.
5. (Cauchy–Schwarz.) Fix J : Fin k → Fin m′. Then Fin.cons e_b (e∘J) = e∘(Fin.cons b J) (compare the entry 0 and the entries i+1, Fin.cases). By step 4 and the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality for finite sums (Finset.sum_mul_sq_le_sq_mul_sq):
   γ_w(e∘J)² = (Σ_b w_b·γ(e∘(Fin.cons b J)))² ≤ (Σ_b w_b²)·Σ_b γ(e∘(Fin.cons b J))² = ‖w‖²·Σ_b γ(e∘(Fin.cons b J))²,
   using ‖w‖² = Σ_b w_b² (EuclideanSpace.real_norm_sq_eq).
6. (Reindexing.) The map (b, J) ↦ Fin.cons b J is a bijection Fin m′ × (Fin k → Fin m′) → (Fin (k+1) → Fin m′) (Fin.consEquiv). Hence Σ_J Σ_b γ(e∘(Fin.cons b J))² = Σ_{I : Fin (k+1) → Fin m′} γ(e∘I)² (exchange the finite sums with Finset.sum_comm, then Fintype.sum_prod_type' and Equiv.sum_comp).
7. (All-tuples identity.) tuple_sum_factorial (with m := m′) gives Σ_{J : Fin k → Fin m′} γ_w(e∘J)² = k!·|γ_w|² and Σ_{I : Fin (k+1) → Fin m′} γ(e∘I)² = (k+1)!·|γ|². Summing step 5 over all J and using step 6: k!·|γ_w|² ≤ ‖w‖²·(k+1)!·|γ|².
8. (Bound for γ_w.) Since (k+1)! = (k+1)·k! (Nat.factorial_succ) and k! > 0, step 7 gives |γ_w|² ≤ (k+1)·‖w‖²·|γ|² = (√(k+1)·‖w‖·|γ|)² (Real.sq_sqrt). Both |γ_w| and √(k+1)·‖w‖·|γ| are ≥ 0, hence |γ_w| ≤ √(k+1)·‖w‖·|γ| (pow_le_pow_iff_left₀).
9. (Conclusion.) By steps 2, 3 and 8: |β| = |a|·|γ_w.compContinuousLinearMap T| ≤ |a|·‖T‖^k·|γ_w| ≤ |a|·‖T‖^k·√(k+1)·‖w‖·|γ| = |a|·√(k+1)·‖w‖·‖T‖^k·|γ|. No restriction on m, m′, k is used: for k = 0 there is exactly one tuple J and 0! = 1; for m′ = 0 we have w = 0 and all sums over Fin 0 are empty, so both sides vanish. ∎

(F2′): by the reused lemma isoperimetric_apply_eq_zero_of_disjoint_support, Z(ω) = 0 whenever tsupport ω ∩ spt Z = ∅. For φ ∈ D^m(U) with tsupport φ ⊆ W we have tsupport dφ ⊆ tsupport φ ⊆ W (SimonGMT `tsupport_exteriorDerivative_subset`), so ∂Z(φ) = Z(dφ) = 0. Source: fact (F3) of the parent proof. The parent justifies (F3) by the singular value decomposition. Transferring that argument to covectorEuclideanNorm, which is defined on continuous alternating maps through the standard basis, would need an SVD factorization L = Σ_i σ_i u_i ⊗ v_i and the orthonormality, for this norm, of the wedges of an arbitrary orthonormal basis. The pinned Mathlib has singular values (LinearMap.singularValues) and an inner product on the abstract exterior power ⋀[ℝ]^n E, but neither the factorization nor any link to covectorEuclideanNorm. The same inequality is therefore proved by the elementary tensor (Hilbert–Schmidt) argument below, which uses only the standard bases.

Notation:
- e_1, …, e_P and e′_1, …, e′_Q are the standard orthonormal bases of ℝ^P and ℝ^Q (EuclideanSpace.basisFun);
- for i : Fin j → Fin P, e∘i := (e_{i(1)}, …, e_{i(j)}), and similarly e′∘i for i : Fin j → Fin Q;
- |γ| := covectorEuclideanNorm γ, so for a j-covector γ on ℝ^m (m ∈ {P, Q}, with the corresponding standard basis), |γ|² = Σ_{I : Fin j → Fin m strictly increasing} γ(e∘I)²;
- L^#α := α.compContinuousLinearMap L, so (L^#α)(v₁, …, v_j) = α(Lv₁, …, Lv_j);
- |·| on vectors is the Euclidean norm, ⟨·,·⟩ the inner product, and ‖L‖ the operator norm.

1. (Sum over all index tuples.) For every j-covector γ on ℝ^m: Σ_{i : Fin j → Fin m} γ(e∘i)² = j!·|γ|².
   (a) If i is not injective, e∘i has two equal entries, so γ(e∘i) = 0 because γ is alternating.
   (b) The map (I, σ) ↦ I ∘ σ is a bijection from pairs (I strictly increasing Fin j → Fin m, σ a permutation of Fin j) onto the injective maps Fin j → Fin m.
      - Surjectivity: for injective i, the tuple i ∘ (sort i) is monotone (Tuple.monotone_sort) and injective, hence strictly increasing. With I := i ∘ sort i and σ := (sort i)⁻¹, I ∘ σ = i.
      - Injectivity: if I ∘ σ = I′ ∘ σ′, then range I = range I′. A strictly increasing map Fin j → Fin m is determined by its range (it enumerates the range in increasing order), so I = I′, and then σ = σ′ because I is injective.
   (c) For such pairs, γ(e∘(I ∘ σ)) = sign(σ)·γ(e∘I) (AlternatingMap.map_perm), so γ(e∘(I ∘ σ))² = γ(e∘I)².
   By (a)–(c), Σ_i γ(e∘i)² = Σ_{I strictly increasing} Σ_σ γ(e∘I)² = j!·Σ_I γ(e∘I)² = j!·|γ|², because Fin j has j! permutations.
2. (One slot.) For every linear functional λ : ℝ^Q → ℝ: Σ_{a=1}^{P} λ(Le_a)² ≤ ‖L‖²·Σ_{b=1}^{Q} λ(e′_b)².
   - Put g := Σ_b λ(e′_b)e′_b ∈ ℝ^Q. Then λ(y) = ⟨g, y⟩ for every y (expand y = Σ_b ⟨e′_b, y⟩e′_b), and |g|² = Σ_b λ(e′_b)².
   - Put u := Σ_a λ(Le_a)e_a ∈ ℝ^P. Then |u|² = Σ_a λ(Le_a)², and by linearity λ(Lu) = Σ_a λ(Le_a)² = |u|².
   - By Cauchy–Schwarz, |u|² = ⟨g, Lu⟩ ≤ |g|·|Lu| ≤ |g|·‖L‖·|u|.
   Hence |u| ≤ ‖L‖·|g| (trivial if u = 0, otherwise divide by |u|), and squaring gives the claim.
3. (All slots, by induction on j.) For every j ∈ ℕ and every j-multilinear map β : (ℝ^Q)^j → ℝ:
   Σ_{i : Fin j → Fin P} β(Le_{i(1)}, …, Le_{i(j)})² ≤ ‖L‖^{2j}·Σ_{i : Fin j → Fin Q} β(e′∘i)².
   For j = 0 both sides equal β()², because there is exactly one empty tuple and ‖L‖⁰ = 1.
   For the step j → j + 1, write tuples as i = Fin.cons a i′ with a ∈ Fin P and i′ : Fin j → Fin P (and likewise over Fin Q). Write Le∘i′ := (Le_{i′(1)}, …, Le_{i′(j)}).
   - For fixed a, the induction hypothesis applied to the j-multilinear map β(Le_a, ·) gives Σ_{i′} β(Le_a, Le∘i′)² ≤ ‖L‖^{2j}·Σ_{i″ : Fin j → Fin Q} β(Le_a, e′∘i″)².
   - Summing over a, the left sides add up to Σ_{i : Fin (j+1) → Fin P} β(Le_{i(1)}, …, Le_{i(j+1)})². After exchanging the finite sums, the right sides add up to ‖L‖^{2j}·Σ_{i″} Σ_a λ_{i″}(Le_a)², where λ_{i″}(y) := β(y, e′∘i″) is a linear functional on ℝ^Q.
   - By step 2, this is at most ‖L‖^{2j}·Σ_{i″} ‖L‖²·Σ_b β(e′_b, e′∘i″)² = ‖L‖^{2(j+1)}·Σ_{i : Fin (j+1) → Fin Q} β(e′∘i)².
   This proves the claim for j + 1.
4. (Conclusion.) Apply step 3 to β := α, an alternating and in particular multilinear map. Since (L^#α)(e∘i) = α(Le_{i(1)}, …, Le_{i(j)}), this gives
   Σ_{i : Fin j → Fin P} (L^#α)(e∘i)² ≤ ‖L‖^{2j}·Σ_{i : Fin j → Fin Q} α(e′∘i)².
   By step 1, applied to L^#α on ℝ^P and to α on ℝ^Q, this reads j!·|L^#α|² ≤ ‖L‖^{2j}·j!·|α|². Dividing by j! > 0 gives |L^#α|² ≤ (‖L‖^j·|α|)². Both |L^#α| and ‖L‖^j·|α| are nonnegative, so |L^#α| ≤ ‖L‖^j·|α|.
   No restriction on j, P, Q is used. For j = 0 both sides equal |α()|; if j > P or j > Q, the corresponding sums over strictly increasing indices are empty. ∎
proof_key_steps: For an alternating γ, the sum of γ(e∘i)² over all index tuples equals j!·|γ|²: non-injective tuples give 0, and injective ones are uniquely permutations of increasing ones.
Single-slot bound Σ_a λ(L e_a)² ≤ ‖L‖² Σ_b λ(e′_b)², via the Riesz vector g of λ, u = Σ_a λ(Le_a)e_a and Cauchy–Schwarz.
Induction over the j slots of a multilinear map gives Σ_i α(L e∘i)² ≤ ‖L‖^{2j} Σ_i α(e′∘i)².
Divide by j! and take square roots: |L^#α| ≤ ‖L‖^j |α|.

Notation. Fix m, j ∈ ℕ and γ ∈ Covector (Eucl m) j, a continuous alternating j-linear map (ℝ^m)^j → ℝ.
- e_c := EuclideanSpace.basisFun (Fin m) ℝ c (c ∈ Fin m) is the standard basis.
- For i : Fin j → Fin m, e∘i := (k ↦ e_{i(k)}) : Fin j → ℝ^m and F(i) := γ(e∘i)².
- S := {I : Fin j → Fin m // StrictMono I} is a finite type, and Perm(Fin j) is the finite group of permutations of Fin j.
- |γ| := covectorEuclideanNorm γ.
The claim is Σ_{i : Fin j → Fin m} F(i) = j!·|γ|².

1. (The squared norm.) By definition |γ| = √N with N := Σ_{I : Fin j → Fin m} t_I, where t_I := F(I) if I is strictly increasing and t_I := 0 otherwise.
   - Every t_I ≥ 0, so N ≥ 0 and |γ|² = (√N)² = N (Real.sq_sqrt).
   - Dropping the zero terms, N = Σ_{I ∈ univ.filter StrictMono} F(I) = Σ_{I : S} F(I) (Finset.sum_filter, Finset.sum_subtype).
   Hence |γ|² = Σ_{I : S} F(I).
2. (Non-injective tuples contribute 0.) Let i be non-injective, say i(a) = i(b) with a ≠ b.
   - Then e∘i takes the same value e_{i(a)} = e_{i(b)} at the positions a ≠ b, so e∘i is not injective.
   - γ(e∘i) = 0 because γ is alternating (ContinuousAlternatingMap.map_eq_zero_of_not_injective).
   Hence F(i) = 0.
3. (Permutation invariance.) Let i : Fin j → Fin m and σ ∈ Perm(Fin j).
   - e∘(i∘σ) = (e∘i)∘σ, and γ((e∘i)∘σ) = sign(σ)·γ(e∘i) (AlternatingMap.map_perm applied to γ.toAlternatingMap).
   - sign(σ) ∈ {1, −1} (Int.units_eq_one_or), so squaring gives F(i∘σ) = F(i).
4. (Parametrization of the injective tuples.) Define Φ : S × Perm(Fin j) → (Fin j → Fin m) by Φ(I, σ) := I∘σ.
   (a) Φ is injective. Suppose I∘σ = I′∘σ′ with I, I′ strictly increasing.
      - σ and σ′ are bijections, so range I = range(I∘σ) = range(I′∘σ′) = range I′ (EquivLike.range_comp).
      - Two strictly increasing maps on the well-order Fin j with the same range are equal (StrictMono.range_inj_of_wellFoundedLT), so I = I′.
      - Then I(σ(k)) = I(σ′(k)) for every k. Since I is strictly increasing, it is injective, so σ(k) = σ′(k) for all k, that is, σ = σ′.
   (b) Every injective i is a value of Φ. Let τ := Tuple.sort i ∈ Perm(Fin j).
      - i∘τ is monotone (Tuple.monotone_sort).
      - i∘τ is injective, as a composition of injective maps.
      - A monotone injective map between linear orders is strictly increasing (Monotone.strictMono_of_injective), so I := i∘τ ∈ S.
      - Φ(I, τ⁻¹) = i∘τ∘τ⁻¹ = i.

   (b) Σ_{i ∈ A} F(i) = Σ_{(I,σ) ∈ S × Perm(Fin j)} F(I∘σ), because Φ is injective by 4(a) (Finset.sum_image).
   (c) By step 3, F(I∘σ) = F(I) for each pair. So the sum equals Σ_{I : S} Σ_{σ ∈ Perm(Fin j)} F(I) (Fintype.sum_prod_type), which is Σ_{I : S} |Perm(Fin j)|·F(I).
   (d) |Perm(Fin j)| = (card (Fin j))! = j! (Fintype.card_perm, Fintype.card_fin). So the sum equals j!·Σ_{I : S} F(I).
6. (Conclusion.) Combining steps 5 and 1: Σ_{i : Fin j → Fin m} F(i) = j!·Σ_{I : S} F(I) = j!·|γ|².

   - for j > m, S is empty and there are no injective tuples, so both sides are 0. ∎
